To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

situational interest contributes little to workbook performance, which in turn contributes significantly to knowledge gain, and that the effect of skipping workbook tasks on knowledge gain is stronger than the effect of performing tasks incorrectly.

(a) students' performance on workbook tasks was positively associated with knowledge gains in learning cardio-respiratory health-related fitness and (b) students who performed the workbook tasks incorrectly gained less knowledge than students who performed the tasks correctly.
situational interest and workbook performance contributed significantly to knowledge gains in health-related fitness knowledge.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of situational interest, cognitive learning engagement, and achievement of students in physical education.
the relationship between students' motivation, cognitive engagement, achievement, and the role of the workbook as a learning strategy in physical education.
the role of motivation and engagement in learning physical education.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
students' situational interest in the learning context contributes little to their learning performance, but it may contribute to the development of cognitive learning engagement and achievement.

students' performance on workbook tasks is the key to learning knowledge, and situational interest is the key to engaging students to perform workbook tasks, which in turn contributes to knowledge gain.
situational interest, cognitive learning, and achievement are interrelated and interdependent, and that the relationships among them are not simple or straightforward.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of workbooks in PE classes can be an effective way to promote cognitive engagement and learning.
situational interest may have an important role in motivating students to engage in physical activity, but not in cognitive knowledge learning in the physical education context.
situational interest and cognitive engagement are both important for students to learn physical education.
The main takeaway from our work is that
situational interest may not be a direct predictor of cognitive engagement in workbook activities.

the situational interest model may be more appropriate for understanding the motivational function of physical activity than for understanding the cognitive engagement and knowledge learning process in physical education.
students' learning is the central goal of physical education, and that teachers should be encouraged to design and implement instructional activities that promote student learning.
